query: For high-entropy alloys used in thermal-insulation applications, what testable hypothesis could be made about an unspecified predictive approach for accurately identifying materials with low phonon thermal conductivity? The hypothesis should explain why the approach would work, predict its improvement over current predictions, define its applicability limits, identify supporting evidence, and specify a decisive experimental benchmark and outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A predictive approach that quantitatively integrates descriptors of local chemical disorder—including metrics of lattice distortion, force‐constant variability, and, when relevant, pore microstructure—will more accurately screen high-entropy alloys (and ceramics) for ultralow phonon thermal conductivity than traditional models. In other words, by incorporating parameters that capture both atomic-level disorder and mesoscale structure, the method will reduce prediction error (by roughly 20–50% relative improvement) in identifying materials with low lattice thermal conductivity under conditions relevant for thermal insulation applications.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys (or ceramics) in a single-phase solid solution exhibiting significant lattice distortions and chemical disorder (and, if applicable, hierarchically porous structures).
generation.intervention: Implement a predictive algorithm that includes descriptors of force-constant fluctuations, atomic mass and size mismatch, and pore structure parameters (for ceramics), and use these as input features for the model.
generation.conditions: Experimental measurements conducted over a temperature range from room temperature to high-temperature conditions (up to 1200 °C) where phonon scattering dominates heat transport; applicability is restricted to systems where the electronic contribution to thermal conductivity is either small or can be separately accounted for.
generation.structural_mediator: Severe lattice distortions and force-constant fluctuations (and, in porous ceramics, controlled pore architectures) that enhance phonon scattering, thereby reducing phonon mean free paths and lowering the intrinsic lattice thermal conductivity.
generation.mechanism: The approach works by capturing both the short-range (atomic-level disorder leading to mass and bond strength fluctuations) and longer-range (pore geometries or mesoscale microstructural features) effects that impede phonon propagation. This dual capture of physical mechanisms—for example, evidenced by the low thermal conductivity in rare-earth zirconate high-entropy ceramics and the force-constant fluctuation effects observed in FeCoCrMnNi—allows the algorithm to better correlate compositional and structural variability with reduced phonon transport.
generation.predicted_outcome: When applied to a representative test set of high-entropy alloys/ceramics, the predictive method will identify candidate materials whose measured lattice thermal conductivities are within a significantly reduced error margin compared to predictions from conventional approaches (targeting an approximate 20–50% decrease in deviation error).
generation.baseline: Current predictive models that rely on standard mixing rules or more limited descriptors, which typically have higher errors in estimating phonon thermal conductivity in systems with strong disorder or complex pore structures.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for high-entropy systems where the dominant phonon scattering mechanisms arise from chemical and size disorder (and structural heterogeneities like dual-porosity). It may not be applicable to materials where electronic heat transport dominates or where multi-phase separation leads to additional scattering mechanisms not captured in a single-phase disorder model.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis extends evidence from porous high-entropy ceramics (e.g., PMC10143762::web::001 and later sections detailing pore-induced phonon scattering) and lattice dynamics in homogeneous HEAs (PMC9726824::web::014), applying those insights to a unified predictive framework. The novel aspect is combining multiple scales—atomic disorder and mesoscale pore effects—into one set of descriptors, and the extent of error improvement (20–50%) remains to be validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a set of high-entropy alloy and ceramic samples that span a range of predicted lattice thermal conductivities using the new predictive approach. Synthesize these materials under controlled conditions ensuring single-phase solid solutions (and controlled porosity if applicable). Measure their lattice thermal conductivity using laser flash analysis and complementary techniques (e.g., TDTR for thin films) over the predefined temperature range. Compare the experimental results to the predictions.
measurements: Laser flash analysis (LFA) for thermal diffusivity
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) for specific heat
X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy for phase and microstructural characterization
Phonon density of states (PDOS) via inelastic neutron or X-ray scattering
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predictive approach does not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in the error margin (i.e., if the average deviation between predicted and measured lattice thermal conductivity does not fall below that of standard predictive methods by at least 20%), or if the model fails to correctly rank the tested samples (e.g., a sample predicted to have low conductivity measures as high), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The unique properties of the porous HECs are ascribed to the high-entropy effects and dual-porosity structures. The severe lattice distortions in the HECs lead to the low intrinsic thermal conductivity by reducing phonons’ mean free path and increasing phonon scattering. Moreover, this results in high compressive strength by inhibiting the crack generations and propagations. The dual-porosity structure possesses several small pores in high-porosity ceramics. These small pores are more efficient in scattering phonon thermal conductivity and inhibiting crack propagations, which are beneficial to improving the thermal insulation and mechanical properties of the porous HECs.

Porous ceramics are often excellent materials for applications due to their low thermal conductivity [,,,]. The ultra-low thermal conductivity of porous ceramics is a primary consideration for high-temperature applications, in addition to a highly stable structure [,]. Great attention has been focused on low thermal conductivity ceramic systems, such as alumina, mullite, yttrium silicate and yttria-stabilized zirconia, which are used as insulating materials [,,,]. However, their further application at high temperatures is limited due to their lower structural stability and relatively high thermal conductivity. Hence, the development of new thermally insulating materials is necessary to cope with the high-temperature applications. Rare-earth-zirconates exhibit low thermal conductivity and good mechanical properties at room temperature, suggesting the potential of rare-earth-zirconates for applications as thermal insulation materials [,]. In recent years, due to better stability, enhanced mechanical properties and countless possibilities in composition design, high-entropy ceramics are already attracting a lot of attention [,,].
